Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Carlos, a 58-year-old forensic analyst who had spent nearly three decades meticulously reconstructing the scenes of other people's worst moments, now found himself unable to step into a building he had never seen before. It had been eighteen months since the afternoon the forensic lab's south wing collapsed. Not an earthquake, not a structural failure anyone could have predicted — a gas line, severed during renovation, had ignited and torn through the corridor where Carlos had been reviewing case files. He had heard the rumble, felt the floor pitch, and then the ceiling tiles had fallen around him like oversized confetti before the fire suppression system drenched everything in chemical foam. He had walked out with a bruised shoulder and a ringing in his ears that no doctor could explain. The physical wounds healed. What remained was a body that would not stop listening for the next disaster.

Carlos’s shoulders stayed tight from the moment he woke until the moment he fell into a restless sleep. His wife, Elena, had taken to touching his arm before she spoke because he would jump if she called his name from behind. A car backfiring in the parking lot of the grocery store would send his heart thudding so hard he had to brace himself against a shelf. He had started to notice that he was scanning every room he entered — looking for exits, checking the ceiling, calculating how fast he could reach the door. This vigilance exhausted him, but it felt necessary. He was certain that if he let his guard down, something terrible would find him. The world, he now believed, was a place where destruction could arrive without warning, through no fault of anyone's — a broken pipe, a careless worker, a moment of inattention. He had always thought of himself as someone who could read danger, who could anticipate what might go wrong at a crime scene. Now he understood that the danger was everywhere, and he could not read it fast enough.

The most concrete change had been in his work. As a forensic analyst, Carlos had once prided himself on being able to walk into any environment — a burned-out apartment, a crime scene in an unfamiliar neighborhood, a high-security evidence locker — and begin his analysis. Now he refused to take assignments that required him to visit sites he had not already been to at least once. He told his supervisor that he preferred to work from the main office, processing evidence that others brought in. He told himself this was a reasonable accommodation. Privately, he understood differently: his reactions since the event proved he was a lousy coper. A competent forensic analyst did not become useless because of one explosion. A man who could not walk into a new building without his hands trembling was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined his career and his identity. Elena had noticed that he no longer offered to pick up takeout from the new restaurant a few blocks away. He said it was too much trouble. What he did not say was that the thought of walking into an unfamiliar place, unable to quickly assess the danger, made his throat tighten.

He finally agreed to see a therapist after a routine fire drill at the office sent him to his knees in the stairwell. The alarm — shrill, repeating — had triggered such a violent startle response that he had dropped his coffee and pressed himself against the wall, breathing in shallow gasps. His colleague had to help him outside. That evening, as he sat at the kitchen table, Elena asked him, very gently, what he was so afraid of. He could not answer. He was not sure he knew anymore. What he did know was that he wanted to stop feeling like a stranger in a world that had become nothing but threat, and he wanted to believe he could be the man he used to be — the one who walked into any room and saw only evidence, not danger.
